title: Structure of Water
description: Discover the secret inside an ordinary water molecule: one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms joined in a bent, polar shape.
keyPoints: One oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms form H₂O.
The O–H links are polar covalent bonds.
The molecule is bent at approximately 104.5°.
Partial charges make water polar.
One water molecule can form a maximum of four hydrogen bonds with four neighbouring water molecules.
funFact: The bent shape prevents the positive and negative charges from cancelling.
examTip: When describing structure, include H₂O, polar covalent bonds, partial charges, and 104.5°.

title: Properties • Universal Solvent
description: Water's polarity lets it dissolve many ionic and polar substances and provide the aqueous medium for cellular reactions.
keyPoints: Oxygen faces positive ions such as Na⁺.
Hydrogen faces negative ions such as Cl⁻.
Water molecules form hydration shells around dissolved ions.
Hydration shells separate ions and stop them recombining.
funFact: A hydration shell is a sphere of water molecules around a dissolved ion.
examTip: State the ion orientation: oxygen toward cations, hydrogen toward anions.

title: Properties • High Specific Heat Capacity
description: Water absorbs a large amount of heat energy before its temperature changes significantly.
keyPoints: Hydrogen bonds absorb energy as water warms.
Water changes temperature slowly.
Large bodies of water moderate climate and body temperature.
Land heats and cools faster than the sea.
funFact: Sea breezes form by day and land breezes form at night because land changes temperature faster than water.
examTip: Connect high specific heat capacity to heat-buffering in organisms and environments.

title: Properties • High Latent Heat of Vaporisation
description: Water requires substantial energy to change from liquid to vapour, making evaporation an effective cooling process.
keyPoints: Energy is absorbed to break hydrogen bonds.
Sweat absorbs heat as it evaporates from skin.
Evaporative cooling prevents overheating.
Transpiration and panting use the same principle.
funFact: Water's latent heat of vaporisation is about 580 cal g⁻¹ in the supplied notes.
examTip: Explain the sequence: heat absorbed → water evaporates → body temperature falls.

title: Properties • Maximum Density at 4°C
description: Liquid water is most dense at 4°C. Below 4°C it expands as an open ice lattice forms.
keyPoints: Water contracts as it cools down to 4°C.
Below 4°C, stable hydrogen bonds hold molecules farther apart.
Ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.
Floating ice insulates aquatic life below.
funFact: Ponds can freeze at the surface while liquid water remains below for fish.
examTip: Use the exact phrase maximum density at 4°C, not maximum capacity.

title: Properties • Cohesion Force Between Water Molecules
description: Cohesion is the attraction between neighbouring water molecules caused by hydrogen bonding.
keyPoints: Cohesion creates high surface tension.
Surface molecules experience a net inward force because air is above them.
Molecules inside the body of water are attracted equally in all directions.
Cohesion helps maintain an unbroken water column in plant xylem.
funFact: Water striders can stand on the surface because of surface tension.

title: Properties of Water • Summary
description: The polar structure of water and its hydrogen bonds explain its unusual properties and biological importance.
keyPoints: Universal solvent.
High specific heat capacity.
High latent heat of vaporisation.
Maximum density at 4°C.
Cohesion between water molecules.
funFact: One molecular structure explains many properties that make life possible.
examTip: Build answers as structure → property → biological importance.
